narrative.summary_main:
- **What your portfolio is for** — Your portfolio should fund retirement and help with college for Liam and Josh. Retirement looks on track, with no gap in the plan. College is the clear shortfall: nothing is set aside, and $113,508.60 is still needed.

- **The numbers in plain English** — You save 22.8% of your income, which is strong. You hold about $150,800 of reachable cash, roughly 16 months of essential expenses, but it earns about 0.09%. About $60,222.50 sits above what you need to hold. Putting cash to work could add about $7,000 a year.

- **Where to act first** — Use part of the extra cash toward the $18,000 card at 18%, then begin college saving of about $4,609 a year. Timothy could add up to $10,500 and Melanie up to $13,500 in 401(k) deferrals this year, which could cut your tax by about $5,760. Moving the brokerage bond fund JNK into a retirement account could remove about $224 a year of tax.

- **One caveat** — Reported expenses look understated, so the cash flow figures, including net cash flow of $36,960.75, are low-confidence. Please confirm your actual spending before committing to new monthly amounts.

- **Worth watching** — Timothy's Roth holds a leveraged fund (UPRO) of $12,740, and technology is 30% of your stock investments. Neither is urgent, but both are worth watching.
narrative.snapshot_main: This snapshot draws on the accounts you each hold: Timothy and Melanie each have their own traditional and Roth retirement accounts, there is a taxable brokerage account, and a separate cash account sits outside the invested total. Your invested assets come to $210,000, with the $150,000 of cash held apart from them. Looking across that invested money, it is weighted heavily toward stocks, at about 77% in equity.
narrative.portfolio_today_intro: The central tension is that the invested money behaves more like a growth portfolio than the Moderate comfort level the household states, and it has to support goals that cannot easily absorb a bad stretch: a retirement both of you are working toward and college years that are coming up for Liam and Josh. Beside it sits a large cash balance that is far more than a safety reserve needs, yet earns almost nothing while an expensive card balance stays open. So the question is less whether the pieces are sound on their own and more whether, together, they are set up to do the job you need from them.
narrative.portfolio_today_what_it_needs_to_do:
- **Retirement income** — You are aiming to retire at 62 (Timothy) and 60 (Melanie), about 21 years from now. The plan is on track: income covers about 93% of your spending need, with $2,371,900.89 left at the end of the plan. You save 22.8% of your income, and both employers' contributions are being captured. The portfolio's job here is to keep that path steady.
- **Education for Liam and Josh** — Liam starts college in August 2038 and Josh in August 2041. Nothing is in 529 accounts yet, and the funding gap is $113,508.60. Saving about $4,609 more a year would begin to close it, so this money needs a defined home and a timeline.
- **Safety reserve and near-term spending** — Your cash needs to cover an emergency reserve of 8 to 9 months of essential expenses, plus the $6,000 vacation in January 2027. That comes to roughly $81,000–$91,000. Your accessible cash of $150,800 covers about 16 months, so this job is more than met. About $60,000 sits above what the reserve and near-term goals call for.
- **Long-term growth for the rest** — The $210,000 invested across your 401(k)s, Roth accounts and brokerage account is meant to grow over a long horizon. Your household's stated comfort level is Moderate, with a 60% stock target, so this money should grow in a way you can both stay comfortable with.
narrative.portfolio_today_what_its_actually_doing:
- **Stock-heavy mix** — About 77% of your $210,000 invested is in stocks, against a 60% Moderate target. Because more of the money is in stocks than that profile implies, your portfolio will swing more than a Moderate profile suggests. Timothy's Growth comfort and Melanie's Moderate comfort are both served by this same single mix.
- **Technology tilt** — Technology is about 30% of your stock holdings, the largest slice, and no other sector exceeds 14.6%. It comes through broad funds, not single stocks, so no one company drives it. Still, a downturn in technology would reach your stocks more than a sector spread evenly would.
- **Leveraged fund** — Timothy's Roth holds UPRO, a leveraged ETF worth $12,740. Leverage magnifies daily market moves, so this one holding can rise or fall by more than the market around it. It also helps explain why that account has been the most volatile of your five invested accounts.
- **Idle cash beside costly debt** — Your $150,000 cash account earns about 0.09%, and $60,222.50 sits above your reserve and near-term goals. Meanwhile the $18,000 Chase card charges 18%, about $270 a year in interest. The cash is earning very little while the debt costs far more.
narrative.portfolio_today_performance_timeline:
Over the three years to November 2026, your household portfolio grew at about 11.7% a year. A diversified portfolio holding the same overall mix of stocks, bonds and cash grew about 12.7% a year, so you finished roughly one percentage point behind it. Your ups and downs were also close to that comparison. The portfolio moved about 7.5% a year around its average, against 6.8% for the comparison. The worst fall was about 9%, and it recovered in 37 days.

The most meaningful pattern is that you moved in close step with the comparison in both directions. In rising markets you captured about 1.10 times its gains, and in falling markets about 1.06 times its losses. That is a nearly even trade, so the difference in return looks small rather than structural. The risk-adjusted measure, which is return earned above cash per unit of ups and downs, was 1.08 for you and 1.33 for the comparison. That is a modest gap. Your 360,000 dollars of assets include 150,000 dollars of cash, which pulls the household's overall stock share down to about 45%. The invested accounts alone run closer to 77% stocks and returned about 20% a year. Timothy's smaller Roth account returned about 41% with much larger swings, which fits its leveraged fund. That result may not repeat.

Two market moments stand out. When tariffs were announced on 2 April 2025, the portfolio fell about 7.1%, against 6.2% for the comparison, so it fell a little harder. A week later, in the tariff-pause rally on 9 April 2025, it fell only 1.6% against 2.4%, and held up better. A third episode, the last Fed rate hike in July 2023, fell about 4.2% against 3.6%. These are only three episodes, and the paths stayed close throughout, so they show a pattern in how the portfolio behaves, not a clear verdict.
narrative.portfolio_today_whats_working:
- **Retirement plan holds up** — Your plan shows a retirement gap of 0, with $2,371,900.89 left at the end of the plan. With Timothy retiring at 62 and Melanie at 60, income covers 93% of the spending need. The goal is funded on today's path.
- **Strong saving habit** — You save 22.78% of gross income, about $61,500 a year. That is above the 20% level often used as a benchmark. This steady habit is the reason retirement is funded, and it gives both of you a base to build on.
- **Employer contributions captured** — Your employers add $14,000 a year to your retirement plans: $6,000 for Melanie and $8,000 for Timothy. Both of you are taking what is offered, so that money joins your own savings each year instead of going unclaimed.
- **Deep cash cushion** — Your accessible cash of $150,800 covers about 16 months of essential expenses, against a recommended 8 to 9 months. It also covers the $6,000 vacation due January 2027. A job loss or medical event could be handled without selling investments.
- **Tax variety across accounts** — Each of you holds both traditional and Roth retirement accounts, and you also have a taxable brokerage account. That gives you three tax treatments to draw on later. Most of the cost of holding bond funds already sits in tax-deferred accounts, such as LQD and SCHP.
narrative.portfolio_today_priorities:
- **Stock weight and concentration** — Your invested $210,000 is about 77% equity against a 60% Moderate target, with technology near 30% of the equity and $12,740 in a leveraged ETF (UPRO) in Timothy's Roth. It will likely swing more than a Moderate comfort level implies, so the risk level needs to move closer to what you both want.
- **Idle cash beside costly debt and education** — About $60,222.50 of your $150,800 accessible cash sits above your reserve and near-term goals, while an $18,000 card balance carries 18% interest. Nothing is in 529 accounts against a $113,508.60 education gap. That cash needs a clearer job across these needs.
- **Low-paying cash reserve** — Your $150,000 cash account earns about 0.09%, so even the reserve you should keep liquid earns very little. Moving it to a competitive cash rate would be worth roughly $2,808 a year while keeping it fully accessible.
narrative.portfolio_today_verdict: Your retirement accounts are doing their main job well: you save 22.8% of your gross income, your employers add $6,000 (Melanie) and $8,000 (Timothy) a year, and the plan is funded with no retirement gap and $2,371,900.89 projected at plan end. The vulnerability is how the money is invested, not how much you put in. Your long-term holdings run at 77.4% stocks against a 60.0% target, Timothy's Roth holds a leveraged fund (UPRO) worth $12,740, and technology is 30.0% of your stock investments, so a market fall could hit harder than your target profile intends. Timothy's Roth returned 41.1% with 30.0% volatility, and that result may not repeat. With about 22 years left for this money, a funded plan is worth protecting from swings it doesn't need to take. You also have contribution limits you haven't reached: since you both already defer to a 401(k), Timothy can add at most $10,500 and Melanie $13,500 this year, which could save about $5,760 in tax. A clear path forward means deciding together how much risk these accounts should carry and which additions fit your cash flow, which we still need to confirm because your reported expenses look understated.
narrative.portfolio_today_also_meaningful: A health savings account is a secondary step for you, best taken after the larger items, such as the 18% card balance, have been dealt with. Neither of you has contributed to one so far, and the household limit is $8,750, so you could contribute up to $8,750 between you. The benefit of starting is a tax-advantaged place to set aside money for health costs, and the savings study puts the tax saving at about $2,100 a year at your current 24% marginal rate. That figure applies only if your health plan qualifies for an HSA, and the data does not yet show whether it does, so checking that comes first. Because your cash flow figures are uncertain and your expenses may be understated, size any contribution to what your monthly budget comfortably allows, and weigh it against your other savings goals, including college. A loss inside an HSA gives no tax deduction, so tax-loss harvesting does not apply there. The data holds no balances, investments or tax-drag findings for an HSA, so there is nothing more specific to say about how one would be held. It is worth agreeing together how much to put in and how it should be invested.
narrative.recommendations_main:
- **Put your surplus cash to work** — You hold $150,800 in accessible cash, about 16 months of essential expenses, while an 8–9 month reserve is the target. About $60,222.50 sits above the reserve and your January 2027 vacation, and most of your cash earns about 0.09%. Keeping the reserve liquid at a competitive rate and putting the surplus to use in line with your long-term plan could add about $7,000 a year.
- **Decide how the 18% card fits in** — Your Chase card carries $18,000 at 18%, with $300 paid each month, while cash sits idle beside it. The interest costs roughly $270 a year. Using part of the surplus cash to retire it could remove a high-rate cost. It is worth talking through together, so you are both comfortable with how much goes there.
- **Start saving for Liam and Josh's college** — Nothing is in 529 accounts, and the funding gap is $113,508.60. Saving about $4,609 more each year would begin to close it, and starting early spreads the cost over more years. Your retirement plan is already on track, so this is the main goal still unfunded. Because reported expenses may be understated, confirm this amount fits your monthly cash flow.
- **Use your retirement-plan and HSA limits where you can** — Timothy could add up to $10,500 and Melanie up to $13,500 more in 401(k) deferrals, which could save about $5,760 a year in tax. If your health plan qualifies, you could contribute up to $8,750 to an HSA, worth about $2,100 a year in tax. Your employer match rules still need confirming.
- **Talk through the level of risk you both want** — Your long-term accounts hold 77.4% in stocks against a 60.0% target. They include a leveraged fund of $12,740, and technology is 30.0% of your stock investments. Your household income is also 38.8% of your net worth. Agreeing on a comfortable level of risk would keep the plan steady for both of you.
narrative.recommendations_scenarios:
- **Three real market events, small differences** — Over the last three years your whole household balance sheet returned 11.7% a year. That is about 1 percentage point a year less than a diversified portfolio with the same overall stock share, and the ups and downs were very similar. When US tariffs were announced in April 2025, you fell 7.1% against 6.2% for that comparison, so a little harder. When the tariff pause lifted markets days later, you fell 1.6% against 2.4%, so you held up better. When interest rates peaked in July 2023, you fell 4.2% against 3.6%. The mixed pattern shows no consistent weakness, and past events do not predict how any future one will go.
- **Your invested portfolio leans toward stocks** — The accounts you invest hold about 77% stocks, against a 60% Moderate target. In a sharp stock-market fall, those accounts may feel the swings more than a 60% mix would. The leveraged fund (UPRO, $12,740) in Timothy's Roth account is part of this. Over three years that account returned 41.1% but moved much more, with volatility of 30.0%. That result may not repeat, and it shows how strongly it can swing both ways. It is worth talking through the level of stock exposure you both are comfortable with. Nothing here promises protection.
- **Your cash cushions the household, not the portfolio** — About $150,800 of accessible cash, roughly 16 months of essential expenses, softens swings across your overall finances. That is why the whole household's worst fall over three years was only 9.15%, and it recovered in 37 days. The cash does not change how the invested portfolio itself behaves in a downturn. A market event could still hit those accounts as hard as their stock share suggests.

rules: These facts are the only figures to quote for these concepts. Quote the label's meaning with the number; never relabel a fact as another one.
Each fact names the facts it must not be confused with. Never call one by the other's name.
Keep the unit: a USD/yr figure is always said per year, a lump sum never is.
Do not add, subtract or compare two facts unless a fact says how they relate.
Never quote a date that is before the plan date.
Write a date as month and year (August 2039), never as an ISO date (2039-08-01).
Write a ratio or rate as a percentage (55%), never as a decimal (0.551).

A fact's `replaces` lists key-metric fields that hold the same or a confusable figure under a misleading name. When you see one of those fields in your other inputs, quote the fact with its label instead. Field names are never labels.

events.name: Fed pivot — December 2023 dot plot

events.description: Yen carry trade unwind and US recession fears triggered a global rout. Japan's TOPIX fell 12.3% — worst since 1987 Black Monday. VIX spiked above 65 intraday. S&P 500 fell ~3% at the open but recovered most losses by Friday. The episode lasted one week.
events.name: Global selloff — VIX spikes above 60

events.description: First Fed rate cut in four years, and an outsized 50bp move, formally marking the start of the easing cycle. Signaled the Fed's confidence that inflation was heading sustainably toward 2% and opened the door to subsequent cuts.
events.name: Fed first rate cut — 50bp

events.description: Trump defeated Kamala Harris decisively. S&P 500 surged 2.5%, Dow +3.6%, Russell 2000 +5.8%. The "Trump trade" lifted banks, small caps, and crypto on expectations of deregulation and tax cuts. USD strengthened sharply.
events.name: Trump election win

events.name: DeepSeek AI shock

S&P 500 surged 9.52% — its largest single-day gain since 2008. Nasdaq jumped 12.16%. Record 30B shares traded.
events.name: 90-day tariff pause rally

events.description: After two days of talks in Geneva, the US and China agreed to reduce reciprocal tariffs from 125% to 10% for 90 days. S&P 500 surged 3.3%, Nasdaq +4.4%. Apple and Amazon led gains as the deal eased supply-chain fears for import-dependent tech and retail sectors.
events.name: US-China Geneva tariff truce

events.description: The Supreme Court affirmed that the Trump administration's use of emergency powers to impose the April 2025 reciprocal tariffs was unlawful, formally unwinding the tariff regime's legal basis. (Exact date to verify on next run.)
events.name: Supreme Court strikes down Liberation Day tariffs

events.description: US and Israel launched coordinated airstrikes on Iranian military and nuclear sites, with nearly 900 strikes in the first 12 hours. Iranian leadership was decapitated. Brent crude surged 10–13% immediately; global equity markets sold off sharply on escalation and energy-supply fears.
events.name: Operation Epic Fury — US-Israel strikes on Iran

periods.character: Fed held rates at 5.25–5.50% for 14 months while inflation ground lower. US equities (led by Mag-7/AI) still delivered strong returns despite restrictive policy.
periods.name: Higher-for-longer plateau
periods.portfolioExperience: Mixed-to-positive: short-duration cash delivered attractive carry, US large-cap led by AI themes, long-duration bonds struggled.

periods.character: After 10Y yield peaked at 5% on Oct 19, cooling inflation data and the Fed's December dot-plot pivot catalyzed a powerful simultaneous rally in equities and bonds through year-end.
periods.name: Q4 2023 rate-pivot rally
periods.portfolioExperience: Strongly positive: both equity and fixed income rallied, rewarding duration and risk after a painful Q3.

periods.character: Three consecutive cuts (-50bp, -25bp, -25bp) took the policy rate from 5.25–5.50% to 4.25–4.50%, supporting risk assets even as the December cut was delivered in a hawkish package.
periods.name: Fed easing cycle — initial phase
periods.portfolioExperience: Positive: equities and duration both rallied through the fall before the December hawkish cut capped the move.

periods.character: Trump's decisive election victory sparked a rally in domestic-focused assets — small caps, banks, crypto, defense — on expectations of deregulation and tax cuts. S&P 500 hit all-time high Feb 19.
periods.name: Post-election "Trump trade"
periods.portfolioExperience: Positive for US-tilted portfolios, especially small-cap and value; international allocations lagged as USD strengthened.

periods.character: Escalating tariff threats against Canada, Mexico, and China — compounded by DeepSeek's AI disruption — reversed the post-election rally. S&P 500 fell 10% from its February all-time high.
periods.name: Pre-Liberation Day correction
periods.portfolioExperience: Moderately negative: US large cap led losses; international equities held up better as the "US exceptionalism" trade unwound.

periods.character: Liberation Day tariffs triggered the worst two-day S&P loss in history ($6.6T erased); the 90-day pause the following week triggered the largest single-day gain since 2008. Geneva truce and S&P ATH by June 27 closed the episode.
periods.name: Tariff shock & recovery
periods.portfolioExperience: Negative turning strongly positive: V-shaped recovery rewarded investors who stayed allocated; international equities outperformed the full year.

periods.character: Repricing away from the 2025 "soft landing + AI boom" narrative toward sticky core inflation, Middle East conflict premium in oil, elevated long-end Treasury yields, and US large-cap underperformance vs. international.
periods.name: Sticky-inflation / geopolitical risk regime
periods.portfolioExperience: Mildly negative: US large-cap drawdown cushioned by international equity, short duration, and energy exposure.
